units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Ah, Ernest has a chin. He has a very strong chin, a square chin. Ernest’s chin is far too square.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: But do you really think a man’s chin can be too square? I think a man should look very, very strong, and that his chin should be quite, quite square.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Then you should certainly know Ernest, Lady Stutfield. It is only fair to tell you beforehand he has got no conversation at all.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: I adore silent men.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Oh, Ernest isn’t silent. He talks the whole time. But he has got no conversation. What he talks about I don’t know. I haven’t listened to him for years.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Have you never forgiven him then? How sad that seems! But all life is very, very sad, is it not?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Life, Lady Stutfield, is simply a mauvais quart d’heure made up of exquisite moments.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes, there are moments, certainly. But was it something very, very wrong that Mr. Allonby did? Did he become angry with you, and say anything that was unkind or true?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Oh dear, no. Ernest is invariably calm. That is one of the reasons he always gets on my nerves. Nothing is so aggravating as calmness. There is something positively brutal about the good temper of most modern men. I wonder we women stand it as well as we do.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes; men’s good temper shows they are not so sensitive as we are, not so finely strung. It makes a great barrier often between husband and wife, does it not? But I would so much like to know what was the wrong thing Mr. Allonby did.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Well, I will tell you, if you solemnly promise to tell everybody else.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Thank you, thank you. I will make a point of repeating it.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: When Ernest and I were engaged, he swore to me positively on his knees that he had never loved any one before in the whole course of his life. I was very young at the time, so I didn’t believe him, I needn’t tell you. Unfortunately, however, I made no enquiries of any kind till after I had been actually married four or five months. I found out then that what he had told me was perfectly true. And that sort of thing makes a man so absolutely uninteresting.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Men always want to be a woman’s first love. That is their clumsy vanity. We women have a more subtle instinct about things. What we like is to be a man’s last romance.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: I see what you mean. It’s very, very beautiful.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: My dear child, you don’t mean to tell me that you won’t forgive your husband because he never loved any one else? Did you ever hear such a thing, Caroline? I am quite surprised.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Oh, women have become so highly educated, Jane, that nothing should surprise us nowadays, except happy marriages. They apparently are getting remarkably rare.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Oh, they’re quite out of date.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Except amongst the middle classes, I have been told.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: How like the middle classes!
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes—is it not?—very, very like them.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: If what you tell us about the middle classes is true, Lady Stutfield, it redounds greatly to their credit. It is much to be regretted that in our rank of life the wife should be so persistently frivolous, under the impression apparently that it is the proper thing to be. It is to that I attribute the unhappiness of so many marriages we all know of in society.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: Do you know, Lady Caroline, I don’t think the frivolity of the wife has ever anything to do with it. More marriages are ruined nowadays by the common sense of the husband than by anything else. How can a woman be expected to be happy with a man who insists on treating her as if she were a perfectly rational being?
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: My dear!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Man, poor, awkward, reliable, necessary man belongs to a sex that has been rational for millions and millions of years. He can’t help himself. It is in his race. The History of Woman is very different. We have always been picturesque protests against the mere existence of common sense. We saw its dangers from the first.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes, the common sense of husbands is certainly most, most trying. Do tell me your conception of the Ideal Husband. I think it would be so very, very helpful.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: The Ideal Husband? There couldn’t be such a thing. The institution is wrong.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: The Ideal Man, then, in his relations to us .
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: He would probably be extremely realistic.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: The Ideal Man! Oh, the Ideal Man should talk to us as if we were goddesses, and treat us as if we were children. He should refuse all our serious requests, and gratify every one of our whims. He should encourage us to have caprices, and forbid us to have missions. He should always say much more than he means, and always mean much more than he says.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: But how could he do both, dear?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: He should never run down other pretty women. That would show he had no taste, or make one suspect that he had too much. No; he should be nice about them all, but say that somehow they don’t attract him.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Yes, that is always very, very pleasant to hear about other women.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: If we ask him a question about anything, he should give us an answer all about ourselves. He should invariably praise us for whatever qualities he knows we haven’t got. But he should be pitiless, quite pitiless, in reproaching us for the virtues that we have never dreamed of possessing. He should never believe that we know the use of useful things. That would be unforgiveable. But he should shower on us everything we don’t want.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: As far as I can see, he is to do nothing but pay bills and compliments.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: He should persistently compromise us in public, and treat us with absolute respect when we are alone. And yet he should be always ready to have a perfectly terrible scene, whenever we want one, and to become miserable, absolutely miserable, at a moment’s notice, and to overwhelm us with just reproaches in less than twenty minutes, and to be positively violent at the end of half an hour, and to leave us for ever at a quarter to eight, when we have to go and dress for dinner. And when, after that, one has seen him for really the last time, and he has refused to take back the little things he has given one, and promised never to communicate with one again, or to write one any foolish letters, he should be perfectly broken-hearted, and telegraph to one all day long, and send one little notes every half-hour by a private hansom, and dine quite alone at the club, so that every one should know how unhappy he was. And after a whole dreadful week, during which one has gone about everywhere with one’s husband, just to show how absolutely lonely one was, he may be given a third last parting, in the evening, and then, if his conduct has been quite irreproachable, and one has behaved really badly to him, he should be allowed to admit that he has been entirely in the wrong, and when he has admitted that, it becomes a woman’s duty to forgive, and one can do it all over again from the beginning, with variations.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: How clever you are, my dear! You never mean a single word you say.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Thank you, thank you. It has been quite, quite entrancing. I must try and remember it all. There are such a number of details that are so very, very important.
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: But you have not told us yet what the reward of the Ideal Man is to be.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: His reward? Oh, infinite expectation. That is quite enough for him.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: But men are so terribly, terribly exacting, are they not?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: That makes no matter. One should never surrender.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Not even to the Ideal Man?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: Certainly not to him. Unless, of course, one wants to grow tired of him.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY
